The test image shows a tomato stem cut longitudinally, revealing very dark brown/black pith discoloration. The outer cortex is green. The interior tissue appears dry and dark. This suggests vascular/pith disease affecting the stem.

Top candidates: Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot, Alternaria_Black_Molds_Stem_Cankers, Southern_Bacterial_Wilt, Verticillium_Wilt.

Let me view reference images one at a time, starting with the most likely candidates.
Both Alternaria reference images were microscopy images. For my 8th view, let me check Bacterial_Wilt stem, as it could show similar internal vascular discoloration.

Now I have used all 8 views. Let me summarize my findings:

**Test image**: Green-exterior tomato stem cut longitudinally, revealing very dark brown/black pith interior. Outer cortex is healthy green; interior pith is nearly black and appears dry/cracked.

**Reference comparison**:
- **Sclerotinia stem** (Bugwood_21, Bugwood_4): Bleached/white outer stem with large black sclerotia embedded. Doesn't match — test image has green exterior.
- **Southern Bacterial Wilt stem** (Bugwood_13): Same structure — green stem cut longitudinally to reveal brownish pith discoloration. Most structurally similar. Color is lighter (tan/brown vs near-black in test).
- **Bacterial Canker stem** (Bugwood_9): Also shows green stem cut open with brown internal vascular tissue. Similar structure, lighter color.
- **Alternaria stem** (Bugwood_4): External dark canker at soil line; Bugwood_13/14 were microscopy spore images — no useful macro comparison.
- **Bacterial Wilt stem** (Bugwood_11): Ooze test in water — not comparable to test image.

**Conclusion**: The longitudinal stem-cut view with internal pith discoloration is most structurally consistent with **Southern_Bacterial_Wilt** — that reference image (Bugwood_13) showed the identical presentation style (green exterior, cut open, dark pith). The extreme darkness (near-black) of the pith also aligns with the description of "dark...brown discoloration in the pith area" at advanced disease stages.
